title: Ultrasonic Testing for Food & Pharma | UT Thickness (US)
description: UT thickness and weld inspection for food, beverage and pharmaceutical plants across the US: jackets, steam, 316L vessels, ammonia piping. Request a UT quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Food, Beverage and Pharmaceutical Plants
html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II ultrasonic technicians to food, beverage and pharmaceutical plants across the United States to measure wall thickness on stainless vessels, jackets, steam equipment and ammonia refrigeration piping, and to examine thicker pressure-boundary welds. Send the equipment list, drawings and your cleaning rules, and request a UT inspection quote. Reports are written for your quality unit, not just your maintenance planner.

What ultrasonic testing is used for in a hygienic plant

A hygienic plant is built around product-contact surfaces that must stay smooth, cleanable and unreactive. Ultrasonic testing (UT) does not touch those surfaces in any way that changes them, which is why it is the first volumetric method plants ask about. A transducer on the outside of a wall sends a sound pulse through the metal and times the echo from the far side. The result is a thickness reading you can compare with nominal and with the readings from the last survey.

In food, beverage and drug manufacturing that answers four practical questions. Has erosion or corrosion thinned a jacket, a shell or a steam line? Is a repaired area still as thick as the drawing says? Are there laminations or large internal flaws in plate that will be formed or welded into a vessel? And, for thicker pressure-boundary welds, is there a planar flaw that visual examination cannot see? Thickness work is by far the most common request, and this page covers it first.

Equipment we measure and what thins it

The equipment list in a bioprocess or food plant is long, and each family fails differently:

  • Jacketed vessels and reactors. The inner 316L shell is protected from product but not from the heating or cooling medium. Steam, glycol and hot water erode jacket plates and dimple welds; thinning of the outer jacket can matter as much as the shell because the jacket carries its own pressure rating.
  • Pure and clean steam generators and distribution. Condensate flow, flashing at traps and repeated thermal cycling thin elbows and tees. These are the first places a thickness grid is worth drawing.
  • Cooking kettles, pasteurizer holding tubes and retorts. Low-acid food retorts are pressure vessels. Shell thickness, nozzle reinforcement areas and door ring welds are routine UT locations.
  • Storage and fermentation tanks. Most have thin walls, but sump areas, manway necks and the bottom knuckle collect chlorides from cleaning chemicals and wash water.
  • Ammonia refrigeration systems. Carbon steel receivers, evaporators and suction lines in dairies, meat plants and cold storage corrode under insulation. UT thickness on the pipe wall, together with removal of a small window of insulation, gives the data your refrigeration engineer needs.
  • Boilers and heat exchangers on the utility side. Steam and condensate lines follow the same wall-loss patterns as in any other plant.

Codes and rules that apply

No single code covers a hygienic plant, so the examination plan is assembled from several. ASME BPE sets design, materials joining and surface finish requirements for bioprocessing equipment, and it is the document your fabricators and validation engineers work from. The 3-A Sanitary Standards govern equipment for dairy and many other food products. FDA current good manufacturing practice rules, including 21 CFR Parts 210 and 211 for drug products and Part 117 for human food, require that equipment be of suitable design, be maintained, and not be reactive, additive or absorptive. None of those documents writes the thickness acceptance limit; that comes from the original design code of the vessel or piping and the owner's engineering.

Pressure equipment is separate. Pressure vessels are built to ASME Section VIII, steam piping to ASME B31.1 or B31.3, ammonia refrigeration piping to ASME B31.5, and boilers fall under the National Board Inspection Code for repairs and alterations. Plants that hold large quantities of anhydrous ammonia are also covered by OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119, which requires inspection and testing of process equipment on a documented schedule. Our measurement method follows ASTM E797 for manual contact thickness measurement and the written procedure approved by an ASNT Level III.

Technique details that matter on stainless and thin wall

Stainless steel is a good ultrasonic conductor, but hygienic equipment adds constraints the generic method text ignores.

  • Couplant. On austenitic stainless we specify couplant that is low in chlorides and sulfur, and on any product-contact side we agree in advance whether couplant may be used at all. Residue is wiped off and the wipe-down is documented so your cleaning program can take over.
  • Thin wall. Typical tank and tube walls are thin enough that a standard transducer cannot separate the surface echo from the back-wall echo. We use small-diameter, high-frequency or dual-element probes and calibrate on stainless steps that bracket the expected range. If a wall is below what the instrument can resolve reliably, the report says so instead of showing a number that looks precise.
  • Jacket access. From the outside of a jacketed vessel you measure the jacket, not the inner shell. The inner shell is measured from inside the vessel when it is open, or at nozzles and manway rims where the shell is exposed. We plan which surface each reading represents before the crew arrives.
  • Surface condition. Electropolished and mechanically polished faces are easy to read but must not be scratched. Our technicians do not use abrasive pads on product-contact surfaces; if an external surface needs cleaning we agree the method with your quality unit.
  • Temperature. Hot steam lines and jackets can be measured with high-temperature couplant and probes rated for the surface temperature, with the calibration block brought to a similar temperature. If the line cannot be safely touched, it is scheduled for a shutdown.

Thicker welds and plate

Most hygienic tube welds are orbital welds on thin wall and are examined visually, with borescope views where the bore is accessible and with sample coupons, as ASME BPE describes. Ultrasonic weld examination makes sense on thicker welds: reactor and vessel shell seams, nozzle welds on heavy-wall vessels, retort shells and ammonia piping at the thicker end of the range. For those, an angle-beam procedure is written for the weld geometry and approved by the Level III before the crew starts. Acceptance comes from the construction code: ASME Section VIII for vessels, B31.3 or B31.5 for piping. Where a flaw is open to the surface the penetrant method on the food and pharma penetrant page is often the faster confirmation.

Magnetic particle inspection is not part of this page. Austenitic stainless is not ferromagnetic, so magnetic particles cannot form an indication, and the carbon steel portions of a plant that can be tested that way, such as refrigeration receivers or structural supports, are handled under our magnetic particle service.

Compare the methods for this plant

Which method answers which question in a food or pharmaceutical plant
QuestionBest fitWhy
Wall loss on a jacket, steam line or ammonia pipeUT thicknessReads remaining wall from one side without opening the line
Cracks or lack of fusion open to the surface on a stainless weldPenetrantWorks on non-magnetic alloys; needs full post-cleaning
Planar flaw inside a thick vessel seamUT angle beamSees below the surface; needs access to both sides of the weld
Surface cracks on a carbon steel receiver or supportMagnetic particleFerromagnetic material only
Internal weld appearance on small tubeVisual with borescopeDescribed in ASME BPE; not an ultrasonic job

What the report contains

Because the reader may be a validation engineer or an auditor, the report is built to be filed. Each report lists the equipment tag or line number, the drawing and revision, the material and nominal thickness, the examination procedure and its revision, the instrument and probe identification with calibration block and date, and the technician with qualification level. Thickness readings are shown on a grid or sketch with the minimum reading highlighted, and a comparison to the prior survey is added when you supply one. Where a flaw indication is found, we record location, length, depth and amplitude reference, and state accept or reject against the code you name. We do not calculate remaining life, set inspection intervals or judge fitness for service; your engineer or authorized inspector does that from our data.

What to send for a quote

  1. Equipment list with tags, materials and nominal wall thickness.
  2. Drawings, piping isometrics or P&IDs for the lines and vessels in scope.
  3. Governing code for each item and the last thickness survey, if any.
  4. Your rules for chemicals, couplant and cleaning in each room, including gowning and entry procedures.
  5. Operating temperatures, insulation, and whether the equipment can be taken offline or opened.
  6. Site address, badging and safety orientation requirements, and shutdown windows.

Planning realities for hygienic sites

Technicians are mobilized to your site for an agreed scope, so the schedule is set around your production calendar, validation windows and changeover cleaning. Entry to cleanrooms and processing areas may require gowning, material approvals for instruments and couplant, and escort. Confined space entry into tanks follows OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 and your own permit system. Washdown areas are wet, so instruments and cables are protected and dried. Ammonia areas need site safety training. We bring our own calibration blocks and instruments; the plant supplies access, lockout and permits.

Where we work in the United States

Pharmaceutical, biotech and food clusters sit in specific regions, and these city pages list the local conditions that matter:

  • Indianapolis has a deep base of pharmaceutical, animal-health and food ingredient plants.
  • Philadelphia anchors a regional biologics and drug manufacturing corridor into New Jersey and Delaware.
  • Newark serves the New Jersey pharmaceutical belt and its steam-heavy utility systems.
  • Boston covers biotech process development and clinical-scale bioreactor suites in Massachusetts.
  • Chicago reaches food processors, bakeries and dairies across northern Illinois and Wisconsin.
  • Omaha is the entry point for meat, dairy and ingredient plants with ammonia refrigeration across Nebraska and Iowa.
  • San Francisco reaches Bay Area biotech and the beverage and wine plants of northern California.
  • Memphis supports food, cold storage and distribution plants in the mid-South.

Train your own technicians

If your maintenance team measures thickness between our visits, UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training cover the method theory, and the ultrasonic simulator lets trainees practice before the hands-on practical at your facility. Under SNT-TC-1A your employer certifies its own people.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, because industrial radiography requires a license under NRC or Agreement State rules. We also do not offer specialist techniques on this page, and we do not decide cleaning validation, passivation or product-contact approval; those belong to your quality unit. For national method background see the ultrasonic testing overview.

faq.q: Can UT measure the inner shell of a jacketed vessel from the outside?
faq.a: From the jacket side an ultrasonic reading represents the jacket plate, not the inner product shell. The inner shell is measured from inside when the vessel is open, or at nozzles and manway rims where it is exposed. We plan which surface each reading represents.

faq.q: Is ultrasonic couplant safe on stainless steel food and pharma equipment?
faq.a: We use couplant that is low in chlorides and sulfur on austenitic stainless and agree in advance whether any couplant may touch a product-contact side. Residue is wiped off, the wipe-down is documented, and your cleaning and validation program takes over from there.

faq.q: Can you measure thickness on very thin hygienic tubing?
faq.a: It depends on the wall. Small high-frequency or dual-element probes resolve thinner walls than a general-purpose probe, but there is a floor below which a reading is not reliable. The report states that limit instead of showing a falsely precise number, and visual examination is often the better tool.

faq.q: Does ASME BPE require ultrasonic testing of tube welds?
faq.a: ASME BPE relies mainly on visual examination, borescope views and sample coupons for orbital tube welds, so UT is not the usual method there. UT fits thicker vessel seams, heavy nozzles, retort shells and wall-loss surveys on jackets, steam lines and ammonia piping.

faq.q: Why is there no magnetic particle page for food and pharma?
faq.a: Austenitic stainless steels such as 316L are not ferromagnetic, so magnetic particles cannot form a reliable indication on them. Penetrant testing is the surface method for those alloys. Carbon steel items like refrigeration receivers can still be examined magnetically under our standalone MT service.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects a thickness reading?
faq.a: The code or specification you name decides, and your engineer or authorized inspector applies it. Our report gives the minimum reading, the grid and the comparison to nominal and to the prior survey. We do not calculate remaining life or set the next inspection date.

faq.q: Can you inspect ammonia refrigeration piping in a food plant?
faq.a: Yes, within the method limits. We measure wall thickness on piping and vessels after the plant exposes a window in the insulation, and we report against ASME B31.5 or the original design code. Plants covered by OSHA process safety management can use the data in their mechanical integrity program.

faq.q: What do you need to quote UT thickness work in a pharmaceutical plant?
faq.a: Send the equipment list with tags and nominal wall, drawings or isometrics, governing code, operating temperature, last survey, your chemical and couplant rules, entry and gowning requirements, and the site address. We then define the grid, probes and calibration blocks and return a scope.

faq.q: Do your technicians work in cleanrooms?
faq.a: They follow the entry rules you set, including gowning, material approvals for instruments and couplant, and escort. Some areas are better scheduled during changeover or shutdown. We confirm requirements before mobilizing so no equipment is turned away at the door.
